practice_notes.statement: In Kerala a scrutiny officer reviews litigant and advocate submissions and marks defects before the file is sent for taking cognizance. Reportedly the role is informal and not in the rules, and the officer often does not mark defects properly, holding files so the advocate approaches him and may make a payment to move the file forward.

claims.claim: a defect-scrutiny step happens before cognizance
the scrutiny role is informal and not in the rules
claims.note: Scrutiny is a formal function: the Registry scrutinises filings and notes objections under E-Filing Rules r.17, and CRP r.68 requires defective petitions to be returned for amendment and representation. Only the specific title 'scrutiny officer' and the file-holding-for-payment fall outside the rules.

claims.claim: files are held so the advocate pays to move them
claims.toCheck: not established as fact; needs field corroboration - who, how often, which courts

relatesToLaw.note: the Registry scrutinises filings and notes objections
defective petitions are returned for amendment and representation

compare.note: Haryana's Panchkula filing assistants perform the same pre-cognizance defect scrutiny at the filing window, but describe it as routine and same-day, without the file-holding-for-payment reported here in Kerala.

attribution.affiliation: Filing assistants, Panchkula lower courts (Punjab & Haryana HC)
attribution.originalSource: Firsthand - PUCAR field interview by Garvita and Varun, 'Interview #1: [P&H HC] Filing Assistants', June 2026. Video: https://youtu.be/RdjhiOHWpUM. Third-party names and the office email address mentioned in passing are omitted.

practice_notes.statement: Filing assistants at the Panchkula lower-court window described how a s.138 ('NACT') case is filed. The advocate submits a physical file assembled in a fixed order - CIS proformas, index, memo of parties, the complaint (its 'prayer'), a Rs.10 court-fee ticket, an attested affidavit, the laminated cheque, an attested power of attorney and a copy per respondent. The assistant scrutinises it for completeness and attestation, enters it in the e-Courts CIS under Criminal then NACT, and the system issues a NACT filing number and a CNR number (HRPK...). The file is registered and carried the same day by a peon to the trial court, where the ahlmad takes over. They also described self-started practices: emailing a PDF copy to an office inbox kept on a desktop folder (unvalidated), laminating the cheque for safety (not mandatory), parking the jurisdictional police station under 'offence remarks' for case distribution, and using Google Translate as an OCR tool for long civil relief text (civil suits, not NACT). For e-filings, only the computer room can release a case into their queue, so they phone it repeatedly; advocates often leave non-mandatory fields (FIR number, police station) blank, which the assistants then fill in.

claims.claim: a s.138 complaint is received and scrutinised for defects at the filing window before it reaches the trial court
claims.method: firsthand account, consistent with the national filing and cognizance scheme

claims.claim: the limitation to file a s.138 complaint is '45 days'
claims.note: The statute gives one month from the cause of action to file (NI §142(1)(b)); the cause of action arises 15 days after the demand notice (§138 proviso). '45 days' looks like a practical rule of thumb combining the 15-day notice window with the one-month filing period, not a statutory 45-day limit. Safe as a conservative check, but it should be computed from the actual dates in each case.

claims.claim: a NACT (s.138) filing needs an FIR number and a jurisdictional police station
claims.note: A s.138 case is a complaint offence with no FIR and no police investigation, so the FIR field in the shared CIS criminal template does not apply to it. The 'police station' the assistants record is used only to distribute cases (by the bank where the cheque was presented), not for any investigation.

claims.claim: a PDF copy of each file is emailed to an office inbox and kept on the desktop as a record
claims.note: A recently self-started, informal practice - not required by any rule and not validated; the copy sits in a local desktop folder. Recorded as practice, not as an official record.

claims.claim: the cheque is laminated at filing
claims.note: An informal safety habit, explicitly not mandatory; its absence is not a ground to reject the file.

claims.claim: e-filed cases can only be released into the filing branch's queue by the computer room, and advocates skip non-mandatory fields
claims.note: An access-control and data-quality gap described firsthand: the branch has no direct release permission (10 to 15 calls a day), and non-mandatory fields left blank in e-filing are re-entered by the assistants. A direct signal for portal design - make the paper-mandatory fields mandatory online.

relatesToLaw.note: the filing and cognizance the window feeds into
the offence being filed as a NACT case

compare.note: Both states run a defect-scrutiny check at filing before the case reaches the court - Kerala through the Registry / 'scrutiny officer', Haryana through the filing-branch assistant at the window. They diverge on integrity: Kerala's note reports file-holding for payment, while the Panchkula assistants describe a routine, same-day, checklist-driven scrutiny with no such allegation.

rollout_states.name: Kerala
rollout_states.note: Mostly individuals and small companies filing. The original clean-sheet pilot - ~2,000 cases/yr in Kollam. Court language: Malayalam.

rollout_states.name: Gujarat
rollout_states.note: High share of institutional filers - banks and NBFCs - sometimes a thousand cases in a day. Needs bulk filing and case management at scale. Court language: Gujarati.
